voiceover.text: Here are three beakers of the same dilute hydrochloric acid, the same volume, at the same temperature. Drop a clean piece of magnesium into one, and it fizzes hard. Zinc fizzes steadily. Copper does nothing. Same acid, so the difference has to come from the metals. How readily a metal reacts is called its reactivity, and observations like these are how chemists put metals in order.

For that order to mean anything, the test has to be fair. Use the same acid concentration and volume, the same temperature, and pieces with about the same surface area. Rub each metal with sandpaper first, because many metals carry a thin coating of oxide that slows the reaction down. Then the only thing that changes is the metal.

So what's the gas? A metal that reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid makes a salt and hydrogen. Magnesium plus two hydrochloric acid gives magnesium chloride plus hydrogen. Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop, and your teacher does that test on a small sample, because hydrogen is flammable. Use dilute acid, small amounts, and safety glasses, in a well-ventilated room.

Add iron to the line-up, and it bubbles slowly. Aluminium foil is a surprise. At first it hardly bubbles at all, so keep that in mind. From the acid test, the order is magnesium, zinc, iron, and copper last, because copper makes no hydrogen.

Water is a gentler test. Potassium and sodium react so violently with cold water that your teacher shows them behind a safety screen, or on video, like in the alkali metals video. Calcium sinks and bubbles steadily. Magnesium barely reacts with cold water, though it does react with steam. With cold water, these make the metal hydroxide and hydrogen. So from water, it's potassium, sodium, calcium, then magnesium.

Oxygen gives a third ranking. Magnesium burns with a brilliant white light. Iron filings sprinkled into a flame burn as bright sparks. Copper shows no flame. It just turns black on the surface, as you saw with combustion. So from oxygen, it's magnesium, iron, then copper.

The fourth test is the most useful. Put zinc into blue copper sulfate solution. The blue fades, and brown copper coats the zinc. Zinc has gone into the solution as zinc ions, and copper ions have come out as copper metal. Now try copper in zinc sulfate solution. Nothing happens. A more reactive metal pushes a less reactive metal out of its compound, but never the other way round. That's a displacement reaction.

As an equation, zinc plus copper sulfate gives zinc sulfate plus copper. The sulfate ions are spectators, so the net ionic equation is zinc plus copper two plus ions gives zinc two plus ions plus copper. Whichever metal ends up as ions is the more reactive one.

Here's a quick way to rank several metals at once. On a spotting plate, put small pieces of magnesium, zinc, iron and copper into drops of each other's sulfate solutions, and count how many each one reacts with. Quick prediction. How many will copper react with?

None. Copper can't displace any of them. Iron reacts with one, copper sulfate. Zinc reacts with two, and magnesium reacts with all three. The more solutions a metal reacts with, the more reactive it is. So it's magnesium, zinc, iron, then copper.

Now put all four tests together. They agree, so they combine into one series, called an activity series: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron, copper. And the acid test tells you where hydrogen goes. Every metal that made hydrogen sits above it, and copper sits below.

Now compare that with a published school series, a secondary source, from the Royal Society of Chemistry. It goes potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, lead, hydrogen, copper, silver, gold. Our order matches. We didn't test lead, silver or gold, because lead is toxic and the others are expensive, so they come from the reference. But aluminium sits above zinc, even though our foil hardly reacted. Aluminium is covered by a thin, tough oxide layer that keeps the acid off. Once that layer breaks down, aluminium reacts quickly. So the mismatch came from the surface, not the metal.

scenes.title: a way to remember the order

voiceover.text: To remember the reference order, there's a silly sentence. Please Stop Calling Me A Zombie, I Like Having Copper Silverware Guaranteed. And the rule for using it, with clean metals in solutions like these: a metal displaces one below it, never one above.

Your turn. Three clean metals, X, Y and Z, were tested. X and Y bubbled in dilute acid, but Z didn't. X displaced both Y and Z from their solutions, and Y displaced only Z. Rank the metals, and say where hydrogen fits. Pause here to answer.

X, then Y, then Z. X displaces both others, Y displaces one, and Z displaces none. Hydrogen goes between Y and Z, because X and Y made hydrogen with acid, and Z didn't. Putting Z first, because it was displaced the most, gets the order backwards.
Last one. A copper wire is placed in silver nitrate solution. Predict whether a reaction occurs, write the equation, and give two observations. Pause here to answer.

Yes. Copper is above silver, so it displaces it. Copper plus two silver nitrate gives copper nitrate plus two silver. Silver crystals grow on the wire, and the solution slowly turns blue as copper ions form. Saying no, because copper is below hydrogen, compares it with the wrong thing. Here, copper is competing with silver.

So observations order metals: how fast they react with acid and water, how they burn, and which metals they displace. In every one of these reactions, the metal turned into positive ions, and a metal does that by losing electrons. Look where the most reactive metals sit on the periodic table: far left, and low down. Why do metal-reactivity trends follow electron removal?
